intro: Every day the dice roll a premise and a dozen constraints, and the game has to honor all of them. Tonight's roll was seed 2593376930, and it rolled a gear who is very, very late. Here's how that became a night up on the Sundown Motel sign.

rolls.value: a gear who is very, very late
rolls.became: The minute wheel in the neon clock on the Sundown Motel sign, fifty-nine minutes late. Not dead, whatever the moths whisper: just late. It's late for a real reason: over thirty years it lost its teeth, and a gear with gaps slips. Every guest who has ever checked out has squinted up at the sign and said “that clock's late.”

The lost teeth didn't go far. They went feral in the dark at the bottom of the sign box, glinting and chattering, and they bite a little when you pick them up. Seat one back in the rim and it's tamed.

Gear teeth are teeth, so the game takes that literally. Some of the teeth in the dark were never gear teeth at all: a denture's molar, a comb's, a zipper's. A tooth's a tooth. Nobody asks whose. Spare tamed teeth go in a glass of water by the sign, like you're supposed to, and every part for the clock is paid for in teeth.
Drag a tooth up out of the dark and drop it on the gear's rim; it snaps into the nearest gap.
Everything stays in the tens: a gear of 60 teeth, then 48, 36, 24 and 12; fifty-nine minutes late, down to one; nothing in the shop costs more than 99 teeth, and the glass only holds 120.
Seconds, the second hand, has never been late in his life. He dares the gear to be on time, once. The loser tells the whole motel the winner is faster.

The teeth think the gear spat them out on purpose. It didn't: teeth fall, that's what teeth do. That's why they hide in the dark, and why they come back in huddles: a tamed tooth tells its huddle it was an accident, and the huddle follows it home. The more teeth come home, the more word gets round, and the more come out of the dark. Every recut sets the misunderstanding off again.
The gear keeps its teeth and loses the dare by a minute. It doesn't mind.
Seconds, the second hand with a smug little face on his counterweight, and the Sundown Motel, where he's always on time and the clock never is.

Five sizes of gear, each its own stretch of the night, about an hour and a half for most players. The moths keep working while you're away (a fifth as fast, for up to two hours), so it plays fine in a couple of sittings.

rolls.value: sacrifice part of your progress to multiply the rest
rolls.became: Catching up is grip times speed, and a gear with fewer teeth turns faster, so the gear has itself recut smaller: 60, 48, 36, 24, 12 teeth. The cutter knocks every tooth out of the rim. Four go onto the drive wheel and the rest scatter back into the dark, sure they've been spat out again, and you tame them back into a smaller, faster gear. The retainer you fitted goes with the outer ring. The drive teeth you buy are the same bargain in small: a tamed tooth given up to make every other one turn faster.

A tamed tooth calms every feral tooth within reach of where it was, and each of those calms its own neighbours, so one drag can bring a whole huddle home, one marimba note higher per link, with a burst of catching up for the chain. Huddles drift together in the dark if you leave them, and the Wind-Up Chatterbox carries the news further.

rolls.value: an ending you have to be talked out of
rolls.became: At twelve teeth the gear gets to one minute late and stops: every gear with teeth has a little slack between them, and this one's comes to a minute (it was on the meter all along). A gear with no teeth has no slack. It would be on time at once, and never turn anything again: a stopped clock, right twice a day (the Toothbrush tried to warn you). The button says CUT THE LAST TWELVE. Each time you press it, someone talks the gear out of it: the twelve teeth, then the moths, then Seconds himself: “It was a dare, not a dentist.”

Everything is a neon tube on brick: the Sundown script, MOTEL, a buzzing VACANCY, the gear, the hands, the teeth. One canvas layer of tubes, blurred twice under itself for the glow, and the script flickers now and then. The fonts are Neonderthaw and Tilt Neon.
Chocolate brick and a dark brown night, with the tubes in its mint, cream and sage, Seconds and the drive wheel in its amber, and the dark teeth in taupe and dusk.

Interlocking marimba patterns in A minor pentatonic, like clockwork that's also a little haunted. The tempo climbs and the layers fill in with every recut, because the gear is spinning faster. Every tooth click, chain and chime is on the same scale, so a long chain plays a run up the marimba.

Glinting eyes in the dark, chattering under the neon buzz, teeth that aren't gear teeth, a wind-up chatterbox nobody wound, and a Tooth Fairy who leaves dimes and won't say where the teeth go. Nothing worse than that: it's a motel sign.
No calendar nod tonight. Late checkout is a year-round thing.

outro: Two sentences: drag a late gear's feral teeth back into its rim, where each one brings its huddle home, and recut the gear smaller and faster four times to catch up with Seconds. Then don't take the last cut.
